hle.note: HLE numbers vary sharply by evaluator and protocol: tool-assisted runs, closed-book runs, and different question subsets are not the same test, and Scale's official leaderboard reports different figures than independent evaluators. The figures here are one named evaluator's consistent protocol. Expert humans average roughly 90% in their own domains.

gpqa.note: Approaching saturation: the frontier cluster sits within about a point of each other in the mid-90s, so small gaps are noise. The human baselines are the context that matters: PhD experts score about 65% and skilled non-experts about 34% even with web access.

mmlu.note: Saturated. Frontier models have exceeded 90% on MMLU since 2024-25, so the headline number no longer separates leading systems, and small remaining gaps mostly reflect answer-format handling and label errors in the test set rather than capability. Current comparisons happen on harder successors: MMLU-Pro, GPQA Diamond, and Humanity's Last Exam.
mmlu.source: Humanity's Last Exam paper (Nature, 2026), which motivates its successor benchmarks by MMLU saturation

big-ann.note: Results are competition rounds, not a running leaderboard: each track (filtered, out-of-distribution, sparse, streaming) has its own winners per round, and hardware budgets are fixed per track rules. Read the per-track results at the source rather than a single headline number.
big-ann.metric: Throughput at fixed recall on billion-scale datasets, per track

llmperf.note: Endpoint measurements, not model quality: numbers move with provider load, region, quantisation, and serving stack changes, so any published table is a snapshot of infrastructure on the day it ran. Measure your own region and workload; the repository documents the method.
llmperf.metric: Time-to-first-token and inter-token latency per provider endpoint

lmarena.note: Arena ratings are relative, not absolute, and the board was re-baselined on July 12, 2026, so ratings before and after that date are not comparable. The board refreshes weekly and the top tier sits within tens of points, where gaps are largely noise. Treat this snapshot as dated the day it was taken and check the live board.

rows.system: Claude Opus 4.8 / GPT-5.5 Pro / Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview

humaneval.note: Effectively solved at the frontier: leading models have reported pass@1 in the high 90s since 2024-25, so HumanEval no longer separates serious coding systems and mostly appears in papers as a sanity check. Current coding comparisons happen on repository-scale and contamination-resistant tests: SWE-bench Verified and LiveBench's coding category.

livebench.note: LiveBench rotates in new questions monthly to limit contamination, so scores attach to a specific question release rather than to a running total, and reasoning-effort settings are listed as separate entries. The top rows sit within a few points.

swe-bench.source: SWE-bench official leaderboard (auto-refreshed daily from the published data file)
swe-bench.metric: % of 500 SWE-bench Verified issues resolved, official submissions
swe-bench.note: Rows are agent-plus-model combinations as officially submitted, so the scaffold is part of the result. Vendor-reported model-only numbers are often higher than official submissions because harnesses differ; the official board is the comparable set.

mlperf-client.note: A downloadable benchmark for consumer hardware rather than a leaderboard: results are published per release and per platform (GPU, NPU acceleration paths), and vendors publish their own runs. Run the current release on the machine you care about; that number beats any table.
mlperf-client.metric: On-device LLM performance per hardware platform

vectordbbench.note: Configuration-shaped: results depend on index parameters, dataset scale, filtering, and the hardware tier each vendor was run on, and the tool is maintained by a vendor in the category it measures (Zilliz). Run it on your own workload before drawing conclusions; published cross-vendor tables are a starting point, not a verdict.
vectordbbench.metric: QPS, latency, recall, and load time per database and dataset

ann-benchmarks.note: There is no single winner to print: every algorithm traces a recall-versus-throughput curve per dataset, and which one leads depends on the dataset, the recall target, and the hardware. The honest result is the curve itself, published interactively at the source, where you pick your dataset and recall floor and read off the frontier.

mlperf-training.note: Results are per-submission-round tables spanning wildly different system scales, from single nodes to thousands of accelerators, with closed and open divisions under different rules. The meaningful comparison is within a round at comparable scale; MLCommons publishes the full result tables per round at the source.
mlperf-training.metric: Time-to-train to a quality target, per benchmark and system

mlperf-inference.note: Results are per-round tables across datacenter and edge suites, closed and open divisions, and very different system configurations, so a single headline number would misrepresent the benchmark. Compare within a round, scenario, and division at the source tables.
mlperf-inference.metric: Throughput and latency per scenario (server, offline), per system
